utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-03-69-T, the Prosecutor versus Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. I'd like to deal with a few procedural matters, not all that I have on my list, but at least a number. And for the first one, I'd like to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. On the 26th of January, the Chamber requested that the Stanisic and Simatovic Defences provide information about the scheduling of witnesses for the upcoming weeks, including the approximate dates the witnesses are expected to testify in court, particularly in light of last week's e-mail correspondence relating to Witness DST-071. Could the Chamber receive an update from the Stanisic and Simatovic Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'm afraid we're not that much further on in terms of certainty. DST-071 is waiting for the service of the subpoena. We expect that that will be done this week, and we've asked WVS tentatively to be prepared to book him on a flight on Sunday for proofing on Monday, to start on Tuesday. That obviously depends upon the subpoena being served and depends upon the witness saying that he is prepared to follow that course. We expect he will, providing that WVS can arrange for him and his wife - he is insisting that his wife comes with him. I think she has accompanied him previously when he has attended court - and he is determined that she does, too, on this occasion. So it's in the hands of the courts in -- in the region --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there an alternative scenario?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I think the alternative scenario is a Simatovic witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Has that been prepared?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, our next witness is already here, DFS-011. He's in The Hague or is in The Hague. And we had some indication that DST-071 should testify next week, so it would mean a lot to us to have a clear situation as soon as possible regarding that witness so that, if that is so, we can take the adequate measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrovic, if he comes, then he comes. If he doesn't come, then he doesn't come. I mean, my question, of course, is: What happens if, for one reason or another, he will not come, have you prepared a scenario. Of course, not the witness who is already here but a witness who could then replace DST-071 if he doesn't arrive. That is the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there is a witness, but it's very hard to tell a witness, "Perhaps you will go and perhaps you will not." There is a witness. We have a list of witnesses and they are coming, but for us it is very difficult to tell somebody that they will be travelling and perhaps they will not be. So this understand certainty as to whether DST-071 will come or not is a bit difficult. If we're told that is he not coming, then we can resolve the problem. But like this, it's very difficult to know about it. So we need to be told this today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, that was my question. Is there a witness who has been requested to remain standby in case Witness DST-071 would not come. And, of course, the sooner we know, the better it is so as to end any uncertainty. That is -- but that's for the next two or three witnesses. I invite the parties to -- to further work on the programme after that. Then following item. On the 6th of February, 2012, in relation to a translation issue regarding P1289, the Chamber instructed the Prosecution in an informal communication to have the translation reviewed and to upload the revised version for the purpose of replacing the present version in e-court; of course, if there's any reason to do so. And that instruction is hereby put on the record. Then the last item. The Chamber has decided on the 10th of January, 2012, to leave the issue of outstanding English translations of source documents of Witness Milosevic's proposed expert report in the parties' hands. On the 13th of January, the Chamber requested the parties, through an informal communication, to notify the Chamber once the issue had been resolved. And the Chamber wonders whether there are any updates.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't have the date in front of me right now, but I can find it. The report has been provided with all the 65 ter numbers marked and indicated to the parties, and the all the documents except for three or four have been given for translation. And as soon a document is translated, it's uploaded, but the document numbers and their markings are available to the parties, both from the Prosecution and my colleagues from the Stanisic Defence. I think a copy was also addressed to the Trial Chamber's legal officer. But we did not receive any response or any requests or comments by any of the parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We were informed by the Simatovic Defence that some of the translations were still missing and some of the 65 ter numbers were also still missing. We are in the process of compiling, actually, the full list of everything that is missing and I anticipate having that hopefully today, latest by tomorrow. I will be sending that in an e-mail. It seems to us that there are actually quite a number of documents that are either not footnoted at all or where the numbers are missing or the translations are missing. But we'll be -- rather than quoting numbers now, I would like to give the accurate complete picture of that, which I will do in the near future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course the Chamber would like to know what the dimensions of the problem are. Could we hear then from you by tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And could I just add, with respect to the military report, we still don't have an English translation. And this is now -- I just have to say that we had estimated approximately three months that we would need to be able to process that report accurately and respond. That was the amount of time that we said in December, in fact. And so as time goes on, that gets to be quite a matter of great concern. I understand that it is in translation but it is now February, and we're quite concerned about that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, after how many years is it now that these reports are still not -- they are not translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my colleague is dealing with that, Mr. Bakrac, and we will inform you about this tomorrow in detail regarding the status of the military expert's report, if you permit us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll hear from you tomorrow. Then, could the witness be brought into the courtroom. And meanwhile -- yes, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could I just raise, very, very briefly, the situation concerning Mr. Stanisic's health.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honours will recall last week the issue concerning where his treatment for his physical condition might be heading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It was on Thursday that a phone call would be made.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes. And I think the phone call was productive, and it looks as though a -- an option has been found, which doesn't, as yet, involve surgery, and that option is a third type of medicine or a third type of therapy which Mr. Stanisic is to start next week in the Bronovo hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that's a medication rather than --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Rather than surgery --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- surgery. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: -- in the Cleveland hospital, which was one of the things being suggested last week, I think. So to that extent, there's been some productive movement, and I think all concerned are somewhat relieved that there is a third option, and that third option, as I've said, will start next week. And I think Dr. van Geenen will file a report - this is what Mr. Stanisic has been told - dealing with the commencement of this new therapy, and also the details of that telephone conference which included Mr. Stanisic's doctor, Dr. Tarabar. That's that. That's the good news. The bad news from our perspective is that after making several requests, at least four requests of the Registry, for all Mr. Stanisic's medical records relating to his treating doctors, we have learnt that his treating doctor, Dr. Petrovic, his psychiatrist, actually has written reports and now the Registry have agreed that we can actually have them. That's after providing us reports without those reports contained therein. The Registry have said that it will take some time to disclose these reports --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me see. "That's providing us reports without those reports contained therein."

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I can clarify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: We've made, I think, four requests now for Mr. Stanisic's treating doctors' reports. On each occasion we have been provided with reports and none of those reports have contained Dr. Petrovic's reports --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. You say in the reports that were provided, those reports were not present.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No. We eventually made a specific request for Dr. Petrovic's report and we've been told, one, they do exist, but, two, they exist in a form alongside other detainees' medical records and it will take some time - so the Registry say - to edit those other reports from the consolidated report. In the meantime, the Registry asked Dr. Petrovic to provide a summary report. We don't know as yet whether it's a summary of the last three years. We don't know whether it's a summary of the last two weeks. We just don't know. What we do know is that that summary report notes that Mr. Stanisic's therapy, psychotherapy, is insufficient. That's as much as we know as yet. Whether that again relates to the last three years or whether it relates to the present situation, we just don't know. We are trying to get answers to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And I just raise that now because, obviously, if his psychotherapy is insufficient, this may well have a short- or mid- or long-term effect on his ability to participate in the trial. That's why I raise that now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That might need some additional attention anyhow because the Chamber noticed that reports by Dr. de Man are not always fully consistent with the reports, that there seems to be some divergence in views, and that that perhaps may have to be resolved as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. And perhaps what I will do in the -- or what we will do is ask Your Honours in the next report by Dr. de Man to comment specifically on the sufficiency of Mr. Stanisic's treatment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay, but we will further look at that. The Chamber is happy to hear also that a -- a new avenue seems to be available for the treatment of the gastroenterology.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Don't look at me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes, no, no. I meant the problems in the field of gastroenterology. Because, of course, the Chamber has considered that a surgery abroad would have some legal implications as well as far as detention or release, or whatever you call it, are concerned and we can put that at least for the time being aside.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not that that's our main concern, to put our problems aside, but, of course, the primary concern is a proper treatment of Mr. Stanisic but all the rest could cause additional problems which we'd rather be without.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then could the witness be brought into the courtroom. Meanwhile, I'll put a few matters on the record. The first one is that on the 2nd of February, by omission, a number D683 has been assigned to document 1D2090. But it should have been document 1D2096, tendered by the Stanisic Defence, and therefore, document 1D2090 is assigned a number, D683. And the document was already admitted as an exhibit. On the 31st of January, the OTP has tendered as video, 2D1001, which was admitted and assigned number P3073. The Registry was informed that the number of the tendered video should be 2D1001.1, and not 2D1001, and, therefore, document 2D1001 should have been assigned number P3073.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Draca.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to remind you again that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony, and Mr. Farr will now continue his cross-examination. Mr. Farr.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Draca. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning. I can hear you, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: I'd like to start by asking you something that you said about the meeting the day before the attack on Skabrnja. And this is at transcript pages 16736 and 16737. You said: "There were no special secrets there. Representatives of the war staff in Benkovac, there was the briefing of the 180th Brigade. We had the chief of the TO staff, the president of the municipality, the president of the Executive Board, i.e., government, and I as the head of state security. When Mladic said that this was unacceptable and that they needed some shaking up, the president of the Benkovac government suggested they should not opt for combat but, rather, that they should make a show of force with tanks and everything else and try through peaceful means to have the various check-points around Skabrnja removed?" Based on this, it sounds like this was a general discussion. Mladic presented the problem and then the other people present, like the president of the Benkovac government, made and discussed suggestions until a final course of action was settled on. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. We didn't even know that he would be there that day. Probably it was just -- he happened to be there in order to plan his daily activities. I assume that they had some sort of strategic meeting that was separate, relating to the status of the military situation on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting you, sir. But I do have a lot of material to get through so I'd ask you to keep your answers as brief as possible if that's okay. One thing I do want to clarify from that answer, however, you said, "We didn't even know that he would be there." Who is "he"?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We didn't know that he was going to be there during the briefing.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And when you say "he," whom are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the man we've been discussing, Colonel Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Can you give us the names and titles of the representatives of the Benkovac War Staff that attended that meeting?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The president of the municipality, Mato Bogunovic; chief of the SUP, Bosko Drazic; TO commander, Zoran Lakic; and myself, as well as the president of the Executive Board whose name I cannot recall now.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And I think that you said that these kind of briefings or meetings took place approximately once a week; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And you also indicated that they lasted at least until the time that Arkan arrived in 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not what I said. They lasted during 1991. And I was present until the state security was dissolved. And it was on the 22nd of January, 1992, that the JNA left Benkovac. So it may have been an error in interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Did some kind of weekly military briefings resume at some point, that you participated in?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did most of the time. But if the brigade commander or his deputies were away, it would be skipped.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And did those weekly military briefings continue more or less until the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I suppose that they did. I can't be sure. It was until November of 1991 that I attended these meetings. But not thereafter.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: So is it your evidence that you didn't attend those meetings when you became either the deputy chief or chief of the RSK DB?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in Benkovac, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Not even during the period between August of 1992 and June of 1993, when you were simultaneously the deputy chief of the service and the head of the Benkovac DB?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let's say that it happened once every month. And mostly in Knin, not in Benkovac. The war-time staff - that's to say, the municipal authorities - I suppose that they did hold them, but I don't know how often.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Later in your testimony you were asked how you knew which units participated in the attack on Skabrnja. And you said the following, at transcript page 16742: "The chief of state security, as the chief of security for that district, I took part in most of the meetings and at the command of the 180th Brigade, in the TO, in the SUP, in the municipality of Benkovac War Presidency." Later in your testimony, you told us that as the chief of the RSK DB, you participated in meetings of the RSK Supreme Defence Council as well as the prime minister's briefings on security matters. Is it fair to say that as a member of the Krajina DB, you co-ordinated and co-operated with all relevant civilian and military authorities regarding military matters during the war?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Your Honours, I apologise for interrupting. Can the witness receive full B/C/S interpretation of what my learned friend put to him? Because some of the elements of what he asked him were not heard in the B/C/S, and I do believe them important for the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I would suggest that you repeat them all and seek to verify whether the answer would be the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: I can do it -- was it just the question or was it the quotes as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question only would be enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Witness, the question will be repeated because it might not have been translated in full. So please carefully listen to the question again and then perhaps you could tell us whether the new formulation of the question causes you to answer the question in a different way. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir, the question I asked you was the following: Is it fair to say that as a member of the Krajina DB, you co-ordinated and co-operated with all relevant civilian and military authorities regarding military matters during the war?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you mean military matters, no. Those were strategic military matters that were only dealt by the commands. We co-ordinated work related to security issues where those overlapped with the issues within the competence of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Jumping ahead a little, during your testimony last Wednesday, you were discussing the Croatian army offensive of January 1993, and, in particular, about the need for more troops. The transcript, at page 16786 -- I'm going to read you a quote and I want to check with you to see whether it recorded your answer correctly. The quote, which is your answer, is this: "At that point, as deputy chief of the department, I attended a number of government meetings of the Krajina where, based on a plan put together by the government, we were requested to provide assistance as soon as possible, and I, in fact, pleaded with the units or with the Main Staff of the VRS, pleaded with them for assistance, but it never came." Was that answer correctly recorded? Was it -- were you asking for assistance from the Bosnian Serb army?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not directly. We did ask for it but always went through the State Security Service of Republika Srpska. We asked them to persuade their colleagues from the army to send assistance to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Why did this contact go through the State Security Service of the RSK and the State Security Service of the RS, rather than from the SVK to the VRS, or from President Martic to Karadzic or Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you remember, I said that, at the time, those were UN protected areas in Krajina, which were not entitled to having an army. However, there followed a period of confusion where everybody was trying to pull the various strings in the services that they had co-operated with. So probably Martic asked of Karadzic and commanders who had their colleagues from the former army would -- would also be contacting them on the same issues, and this is how it would happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: But why was the state security involved?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, as was the case with all the other security institutions, we, too, were charged with security in the Republic of Serbian Krajina. Even though we didn't have other own military formations, we could use our good co-operation and influence with the colleagues in Republika Srpska to secure a number of units. Unfortunately, we failed in that effort.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: You said you didn't have your own military formations. To your knowledge, was the RSK DB ever involved in efforts to obtain weapons for the SVK or for other armed forces in the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know about that. Even the official weapons we had had arrived -- were ordered and arrived from the RSK Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And what about the Serbian DB? To your knowledge, was the DB of the Republic of Serbia ever involved in attempts to obtain weapons for the SVK or other armed forces in the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir, I'd now like to summarise some of your evidence about your relationship with Milan Martic and I'd ask you to tell me if I get anything wrong. You said you met with Martic when the SAO Krajina DB was being formed. You met with Martic around the time that Captain Dragan was setting up the training centre at Golubic. You met with him after the massacre at Bruska. You met with him when the RSK DB was being reformed in late 1992. You went with him to see Fikret Abdic on two occasions, and Martic was the one who informed you about the creation of the Pauk Command. Is all of that correct?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: So based on that, is it fair to say that you had close professional co-operation with Mr. Martic?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Your Honours, could we move into private session briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir, on Thursday, you were asked a number of questions about the facilities and people at Erdut, as well as some units that may have been stationed there. As far as you know, did any RSK official ever indicate, either to you or to anyone else, that the DB of Serbia controlled an armed group at Erdut?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nobody ever told me anything like that. This was under the control of the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina formally and legally speaking, though I know that Arkan's units were in there. And the education centre was within the competence of the Ministry of Defence and Ministry of the Interior of the RSK.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And, sir, you've told us that nobody ever told you anything like that. But did you ever hear about an RSK official saying to someone else that the Serbian DB controlled an armed group at Erdut?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I can say that, as far as I know, the DB of Serbia had no influence over the centre. At least not directly so. Whether they had any agents there, I cannot possibly know.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And, again, to your knowledge, did any official of the RSK government ever state or claim that Rade Kostic was a member of the state security department of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Many claimed that the late Rade Kostic was a member of the DB of Serbia but nobody was sure of it. We weren't present in the field at the time he formally worked for the Ministry of the Interior of the RSK. Whether he carried an ID and had an actual employment with the DB of Serbia is something that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A part of witness's answer was not recorded as to who was present in the field and how far. What we have in the transcript does not reflect what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Having heard the comment of Mr. Petrovic, could you please repeat your answer in respect of who was present in the field and how far -- I have some difficulties in ... Could you please repeat that portion of the answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I was mentioning Erdut, perhaps I misspoke when I said "we were not present in the field." I meant the Ministry of the Interior or, rather, state security. You have to understand that Eastern Slavonia and Baranja are physically separated and some 6- to 700 kilometres away from Knin. You had to go through Bosnia-Herzegovina and partly through Serbia to reach there. And it was difficult for us to go out into the field. I think that it was in late 1992 that I went there for the first time. We weren't physically present there. There were deputy and assistant defence ministers up there who would inform us of the goings on through dispatches and by phone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you one additional question in relation to one of your previous answers. You said: "Many claimed that the late Rade Kostic was a member of the DB of Serbia but nobody was sure of it." Could you give us some more details about who claimed that Rade Kostic was, and why that person wasn't certain, and when you learned about that claim.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it was simply talked of by people in general and in the police circles. But I have to tell you that the story went about about me being a member of the DB of Serbia. I have to tell you that nobody told me that he had been working for the DB of Serbia. At least I wasn't aware of it. I don't know it, still, to this day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. But -- but when did you learn about those claims? Who told you about that story going around?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, truthfully, it's very difficult 20 years on to know who exactly it was who was saying. But it was in the grape-vine. The story was talked about mostly in the police circles. Let me stress that the same sort of stories circulated in respect of most of the officers working for state security.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Most of what officers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And that was already claimed at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you know how it is. Serbia is a large country compared to us. Some people perhaps found it suitable. Some may have started the stories themselves. But as for Rade Kostic, I cannot say that I knew for sure that he was a worker working permanently for the DB of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Where you earlier said, when you were asked about the Serbian DB, whether they controlled an armed group at Erdut, your answer was: "No. I can say that -- I can say that, as far as I know, the DB of Serbia had no influence over the centre. At least not directly so. Whether they had any agents there, I cannot possibly know." Do I now understand that the full answer to that question would have been: Whether they had any agents there, I cannot possibly know, but rumours went around that some of the officers, including Kostic, were members of the DB of Serbia? It's not -- it's not knowledge about Kostic and other officers being employed by the DB of Serbia, but you were aware of rumours which claimed that they were. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. As rumours. That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did you ever contradict -- you said it was even said about you. Did you ever contradict that to anyone? Did you ever make a public statement, "I am not in whatever way related to the Serbian DB"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, more than once. Especially if the question came from somebody who was close to me or from the media. Then I would adamantly deny it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did you ever try to find out what was true in those rumours and what was not true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I didn't try to do so. I said that there were such rumours going around for so many people, including the army. It was pointless to try to check if it was true, to either confirm or deny it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Farr.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to just briefly follow up on one of Judge Orie's questions. He said: Can you give us some more details about who claimed that Rade Kostic was and why that person wasn't certain and when you learned about the claim. Your answer was: "Well, it was simply talked of by people in general and in the police circles." I want to make sure I understand your evidence. Is it your evidence that you can't recall any person in particular who mentioned that?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir, are you aware that on the 20th of April of 1991, a decision was published in the SAO Krajina gazette that purported to join the territory of the SAO Krajina to the territory of the Republic of Serbia? Just are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were difficulties in interpretation, but it's been sorted out. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. Could you please answer the question, whether you were aware of the decision which was published in the SAO Krajina gazette.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It was widely published by all the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And as an official of the SAO Krajina and later of the RSK, did you personally share that goal of joining the RSK to Serbia?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that point in time, I was not an official yet. Apparently the Assembly in Serbia, in Belgrade, rejected it, so it seemed moot for us down there to be entertaining the idea at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: During the time that you were the head of the RSK DB, was there ever any plan or proposal to join the RSK DB to the DB of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was never such a plan. I absolutely assert that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Could we please have 65 ter 6366 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir, this document is the work report of the RDB of the RSK MUP for 1993. It's dated 25 April 1994 and it's addressed to the minister of the interior and the government of the RSK. If we could now have the middle of page 3 in B/C/S and the middle of page 4 in English. And, sir, for the moment, can you just confirm that that's your signature and your stamp at the bottom of that document?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is my signature and stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Okay. Can we now please have the bottom of page 2 in B/C/S and the middle of page 3 in English. And, sir, I'm just going to read a portion of the document to you and ask you to comment on it. I'm interested in the portion that says: "In the same period, 52 reports were submitted to the president of the republic and the government of the RSK, while 64 information regarding the military issues have been submitted to the Main Staff of the VRSK ..." Are you able to tell us why the number of reports submitted to the Main Staff of the SVK is slightly higher than the number of reports submitted to the RSK government?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we're talking about sending them to the government and the president, that often was once a week, an overview. As for the others noted here, these were operative matters, so sometimes there would be two or three dispatches per day, if the situation required that. In one day.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: The document goes on to say: "118 reports, dispatches, memos, Official Notes have been submitted to the 2nd Administration of the Republic of Serbia MUP and 28 information to the RDB of the Republika Srpska MUP ..." Dealing first with the 118 reports sent to the 2nd Administration of the Republic of Serbia MUP. To be more precise, that's actually a reference to the 2nd Administration of the DB of Serbia; correct?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. But this is 118 different reports for the 1st and the 3rd Administration. I don't know why that was not stated here. But a large part of that was sent to the 2nd Administration, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: On Thursday of last week, I asked you whether you sent more reports to your own government or to the 2nd Administration of the DB of Serbia. Your answer was: "We sent an immeasurably larger number of reports to the government. When I say 'the government,' I mean the president of the republic. We were obliged on a daily basis to make a cross-analysis of all of the political events and these reports were issued daily. Then there were weekly separate reports which were a compilation of all this information. We did not have such a voluminous contact with the 2nd Administration." Sir, this report contradicts that testimony, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you look carefully at this report, it says 52 reports to the president of the republic. These are the weekly reports. But the daily reports are not mentioned here, and the president would know that there were 365 of them in a year.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Why wouldn't you --

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were even sent on a Sunday.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Why wouldn't you have mentioned the daily reports in this year-end report?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know where the -- this document is from. Perhaps it's just been deleted. Perhaps at that point in time we didn't think it was important to mention that. I think that even for the Main Staff there were more than -- more reports than is stated here, more than these 64.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: You've just said: "Perhaps at that point we didn't think it was important to mention that." Is it your evidence that while you did send more reports to the president and the government, you sent more important reports to the 2nd Administration of the Serbian DB? Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand you properly. How -- how do you explain that?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Why wasn't it important to mention the daily reports in this year-end report?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would take the daily reports to the president myself, personally. Every day between 9.00 and 10.00 in the morning, I had a briefing with him. If I was on a trip somewhere, then my deputy would take them. So we probably thought that these analytical reports were more important that were prepared by the analysis department and that was sent to the president by mail on a weekly basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: You've just said these analytical reports were more important. In other words, the weekly reports were more important. So is it your evidence that, while you may have sent more reports to the government of the RSK, you sent more important reports to the 2nd Administration of the Serbian DB than you did to the government of the RSK?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you're trying to tell me is technically impossible. Why would the 2nd Administration need something that needed to be acted upon urgently? That would have been better sent to our government. 20 years on I cannot really evaluate which reports are more important, the daily or the weekly ones. Events were following one upon the other. It was a situation of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, I'm just going to tell you the Prosecution position and ask for your comment and then I'll move on. It's our position that the large number of documents sent from the RSK DB to the 2nd Administration of the DB of Serbia shows that the co-operation between the two services went beyond the normal co-operation between friendly services. And, in fact, for practical purposes, the RSK DB and the DB of Serbia were functioning almost as a single service. Just if you would like to respond to that.

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I still assert that that is not correct. But I have to add that, unfortunately so.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Can we now have the middle of page 4 in English and the middle of page 3 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And, sir, directing your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Sorry. Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Is it possible to have a break? I know that this next section might take a little while. And I'm also wondering whether it might be fair to allow the witness to read the whole report to remind himself of what this report says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Farr.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wouldn't have any objection to that. We can probably provide a printed copy to ... whom would we provide a printed copy to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think to the Registry. The Registry would then take care that -- the Registrar will take care that it ends up in the hands of the witness. And then, I take it, a B/C/S version will be provided to him. We'll take a break, and I'd like to briefly - after having discussed it with my colleagues - to raise a matter with counsel of all three parties, but primarily Mr. Jordash being involved, on a matter which was just brought to my attention a minute ago. So if you would remain standby so that if I would like to hear information from you, that I could receive that. We take a break, and we resume at a quarter to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't see any witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Farr, if you're ready, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir, before the break, we were looking at the 1993 work report of the RSK DB. Just before we started looking at that document, I asked you a question, and I want to repeat that for you, along with your answer. The question, at page 23 of the transcript, was: "During the time that you were the head of the RSK DB, was there ever any plan or proposal to join the RSK DB to the DB of Serbia?" Your answer was: "No. There was never such a plan. I absolutely assert that." I would now like to read you to the last sentence in the 1993 report of the RSK DB. It says: "It might be that due to the problems of the organisational nature no significant results in the intelligence work have been achieved. However, it can be said that the foundation for the serious work and the final preparations for the annexation to the RDB of the Republic of Serbia MUP has been created." Sir, to me, that seems like a complete contradiction. Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can explain. I repeat with full responsibility that I never wrote a single document, nor did I receive a document from anyone, nor did I attend any meeting where the possibility of annexing the RDB of the Republic of Serbia to us or, actually the other way around, us to the RDB of Republic of Serbia, was discussed. This sentence of mine and my formulation is here. The report was made on the basis of an analytical overview. I wrote this sentence and the reason for that I have to explain in -- this was in order to relieve the pressure of President Martic towards me, or towards the service, rather. He had a great desire for all the ministries in the Krajina, especially the national bank, financial institutions, the Public and the State Security Service, he wanted to annex them all to the government of the Republic of Serbia. Since at that time he was not on good terms with Mr. Stanisic, the chief of the RDB of Serbia, he always exerted pressure on me to initiate that, because I knew, for technical and political reasons, that I was unable to do that. I never initiated this, but I had to -- I mean, I didn't have to but I just thought I had to ease the pressure a little bit, and I had to explain to him, hopefully, that this was not possible. If you look at this report carefully, it is addressed exclusively to the minister of the interior who is the initiator of the idea for us to make an overview which then he would be able to take to Martic. I knew that this was so and, simply, I put that there because of the minister and because of Martic. If we look at the previous paragraph, we can see how small the funds were that we got from the government budget for our work. I mean, if there were any serious preparations, we would receive some funds from the RDB of Serbia and not -- we would not only have had 27.000 German marks for our work throughout that whole period. I hope you understand. These were completely different times. It was war. Again, I repeat, the president was what he was. So I had to cope with this in -- in different ways. Also, I would like to add - I assume that the archives are accessible to you - I'm convinced that you will not find a single document that talks about the joining or merger of these two services.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir, in that answer, when you were talking about President Martic, you said: "He had a great desire for all the ministries in the Krajina, especially the national bank, financial institutions, the Public and the State Security Service, he wanted to annex them all to the Republic of Serbia ..." Sir, that is a plan or a proposal to annex the RSK DB to the DB of Serbia, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was his idea. But technically, neither orally or in writing did we ever initiate such initiatives, and I never had an opportunity to discuss this topic with Mr. Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Did Mr. Martic ever propose that idea to you? That the RSK DB be annexed to the DB of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, frequently. Even though I tried to explain to him that this was impossible without a parliament decision, and without the decision of the Government of Serbia. But he had frequent misunderstandings at that time with President Milosevic and he felt that he could link up with Serbia through the back door, in order to place Milosevic before a fait accompli. But I knew that this was not -- that this was impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: What were the final preparations for the annexation of the RSK DB to the DB of Serbia? What did you do?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again, I repeat, I claim that there were no preparations at all for that. I am personally responsible for this formulation here. And I've already explained why that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't understand that. How -- how does -- how does final preparations match with no preparations? I didn't get that from your answer.

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I put that there, that formulation, that wording, in order to satisfy the president, but there were no preparations whatsoever, which implies no final preparations either.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: So you lied to the president of your republic.

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't directly lie to him, but I was guided by the desire to ease the pressure. Because his calls frequently were on a daily basis, and he was known as a man who was difficult to co-operate with. So in order to avoid misunderstandings with him, I did that, in order to prevent any obstructions to our work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Draca, you're actually explaining why you didn't tell him the truth, isn't it? And whether we call that a lie or not, the truth, that's, of course, I would say a semantic issue. And you're just explaining that what you wrote down here - that's how we understand your testimony - was not the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You could put it that way, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Can we please have P987 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And talking about the truth, et cetera, you explained to us now several times that Mr. Martic insisted so much on planning to join the RSK institutions to the Republic of Serbia institutions. That should have been part of your answer when you were asked about whether any plans were -- or proposals were made. Because after you had denied that ever such plans were there, not talking about proposals, you now explain to us that Mr. Martic had proposed this various times. And that should have been part of your answer on the first question put by Mr. Farr. Because you are not only supposed to tell us the truth and nothing the truth, but also the whole truth, and this was part of what you explained to us now to be the truth. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Your Honour, I neglected to tender that last document. It's 65 ter 6366, and I'd ask that it be admitted as a Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the 1993 report.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 65 ter 6366 will receive number P3076, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And, absent any objections, is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir, on your screen we have a letter dated 7 October 1994 written by Milan Martic. It's addressed to Slobodan Milosevic, the president of Serbia; to Mirko Marjanovic, the prime minister of Serbia; Zoran Sokolovic, the minister of the interior; and to General Perisic, the chief of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia. It concerns an incident on the 4th of October of 1994 when Martic was threatened by armed men after crossing the border from Serbia into the RSK. Following the incident, Martic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you reading at this moment? Then could we please have the English version, because I see that it appears in the B/C/S but -- yes, there we are.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Your Honour, in fact, I was paraphrasing. I will be quoting a portion of the letter. But to continue the paraphrase. Following the incident, Martic went to the command of the 11th Corps in Vukovar. And if we could now have the middle of page 3 in English and the top of page 2 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are we able to allow the witness somehow to read the entire document, so he has an idea of what the whole document is about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I think Mr. Farr has introduced the document. If there's -- if there's any aspect of this document you would consider it useful at this stage, not later in your examination, to be put to the witness, then you may do a suggestion to Mr. Farr. Please proceed, Mr. Farr.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir, the portion that I'm interested, and I'll read that part verbatim, it says: "At the meeting in the command of the 11th Corps in Vukovar, I was given the following information. The men who organised the incident were members of the paramilitary and parapolice forces stationed in Erdut. They are under the direct control of Rade Kostic of the state security department of the MUP of Serbia. These individuals also took part in the kidnapping of Ilija Prijic, minister of the interior of the RSK. "The said Rade Kostic had entered the territory of the RSK an hour before I did, i.e., at about 0900 hours, in an official BMW with registration plates of the MUP of Serbia."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the counsel please provide a reference in the B/C/S, in the original, for the sake of the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: This is the top of page 3 in English and the middle of page 2 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm ... yes. The second paragraph in English about the Pajero is found on the top of the page in B/C/S. And Mr. Farr started reading a little bit further down at the end of the first paragraph in B/C/S, the 11th Corps. Is there any need to have it read again by ...?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. At least the second part of the counsel's question.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Yes, I'll read the -- the second portion. "The said Rade Kostic had entered the territory of the RSK an hour before I did, i.e., at about 0900 hours, in an official BMW with registration plates of the MUP of Serbia." And if we could now have the middle of page 4 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: There's no page 4 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: That would be the middle of page 4 in English - I apologise - and the bottom of page -- the bottom of page 2 in B/C/S. And for the booths' information, I will be starting to read with the paragraph that says: "Mr. President of the Republic ..." Second from the bottom in the B/C/S version. This portion says: "Mr. President of the Republic, Mr. Prime Minister, Minister of the Interior, Chief of Staff, my decision at present is not to go public with everything that happens to me in the state of which I am the president. There is overwhelming evidence that the state security of the MUP of Serbia is behind these paramilitary and parapolice forces. There is also irrefutable evidence that in 80 per cent of the cases these men come from the Republic of Serbia. "I have evidence to support all of the above."

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir, you knew about these claims by Milan Martic; correct?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did. I knew about this incident. Immediately on his return, Martic convened the Supreme Defence Council to discuss this incident. I'm not familiar with this document though. I'm seeing it for the first time. But I do know what he said about it and it was similar, and then he issued orders in relation to that. I can say that this incident was a result of the political conflict between Hadzic and Martic because Rade Kostic or anyone else would prevent the president from entering the area of Slavonia. Why would that be in the interests of the Serbian state security? Since the minister of interior is not mentioned here but he was with Martic. He did not wish to call anybody to Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, lines 13 to 16, page 36. I think that that is incomplete. The witness explained whose role -- who had what role there. At least that's how I understood it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: If I may. It's one situation where Mr. Petrovic is completely certain that a particular word has been left out or some concrete identifiable mistake has been made, but where we're dealing with his understanding of a witness's answer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If he says that the witness explained beyond what is translated to us, then he is fully entitled to raise that matter. What I'll do, Mr. Draca, I will read the answer as it appears on the transcript. Now, if there's anything left out, I don't want you to tell us why or, et cetera, but just to add what is not there but what you did say. I slowly read what we find on our transcript. "I can say that this incident was a result of the political conflict between Hadzic and Martic because Rade Kostic or anyone else would prevent the president from entering the area of Slavonia. Why would that be in the interests of the Serbian state security?" Is there anything missing in what I just read?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that we discussed the issue at the collegium meeting of the Supreme Defence Council. For the rest, I really don't know. But that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't want to make suggestions, but the witness did draw a distinction between what Rade Kostic could and could not do. But this can easily be checked. I wouldn't want to suggest anything. We can have the tape checked and then we will see what the witness had to say on the issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At the same time, I think Mr. Farr would appreciate if you informally would tell him what, in your view, is missing so that Mr. Farr, if it is of any relevance for his follow-up questions, but perhaps you could send him an e-mail or -- what you think is missing. And apart from that, we can check the audio at a later stage, if there's any reason to do that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir, you've just indicated that you knew about this incident immediately upon Martic's return, that he convened the Supreme Defence Council to discuss the incident, and that you know what Martic said about it. Earlier today, and this is at page 18 of the transcript, I asked you: "As far as you know, did any RSK official ever indicate either to you or to anyone else that the DB of Serbia controlled an armed group at Erdut?" Your answer was: "No. Nobody ever told me anything like that. This was under the control of the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Serbian Krajina." And then you went on to give your view of who was in control of the facility of Erdut. Sir, again, to me, there seems to be a total contradiction between what you just said about Martic having told you about this incident and then what he said about it, and you never having been told anything about the DB Serbia controlling an armed group at Erdut by any RSK official. Could you please explain that?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't finish off my answer, really, because Mr. Petrovic interrupted me. On that occasion, Martic did not say decidedly that he knew which units were involved and I was just about to say that he tasked the minister of the interior with that matter because they didn't think it appropriate that they should talk to these people. So I was asked to call Mr. Kostic because the information he received from the army, that's to say, from the 11th Corps command, seemed quite lacking conviction. For instance, he was the deputy minister of the interior for Baranja, which is an area north of East Slavonia. So especially when it comes to Erdut, Kostic had no powers whatsoever over that particular centre. So I did call Rade Kostic after this incident, and he said that he had no part in it, that the 11th Corps command was deceiving Martic, that on that same evening when Martic left, they talked to Hadzic. And the story was that they were between two stools. Anyway, subsequently Martic met up with Hadzic. They sorted it all out without actually going into the details as to whose unit these members belonged to. This is the first time I'm looking at this report. Since I'm the chief of -- since I was the chief of the State Security Service, I issued an order without the knowledge of Mr. Martic, asking that the service in East Slavonia and Baranja shed more light on this event. They told me that there was a written report somewhere which said that these were members of public security who were under full control of Hadzic. Lest I should create more clashes and conflicts, I did not forward this report to the president of the republic. And when I say "clashes or conflicts," I mean of political nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir, I want to be sure that understand your testimony. Martic did tell you that he believed that it was members of the State Security Service of Serbia who were responsible for this; correct?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He didn't put it that way. He said that he had heard from the 11th Corps command that they were members of the MUP of Serbia. But we expressed our disbelief at that very meeting. It seemed unlikely that anyone from Serbia would be coming, since the RSK MUP and the 11th Corps in -- had enough members in Slavonia who were loyal to that structure higher up. I don't see why anybody would be calling people from Serbia to come on in.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir, if you -- if you corrected, as you say, Martic's information, why did he then send a letter to Slobodan Milosevic, among others, claiming that these were people under the control of the State Security Service of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that this is the first time I'm looking at this report. Perhaps he was acting on an impulse and asking President Milosevic for help, because his reasoning was that if this was true, only the state leadership of Serbia could give him an answer to that question. I really don't know what his motivations were. Knowing him, I suppose that this is it what they told him, because he was not a man given to making things up --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness repeat what he said last.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir, the end of your answer was not recorded. Could you repeat whatever the last thing you said was.

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that Martic was given to accepting disinformation which would oftentimes result in political clashes in RSK, but not only within the RSK but also political conflicts with the RS and Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir, knew that Mr. Martic did, in fact, send this letter, correct, and you knew what the contents were, generally speaking?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I've said twice already that this is the first time I'm looking at this letter. I wasn't aware of this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: So just to be clear, it's your evidence that at a time when you were the chief of state security of the RSK, when you were, as you say, reporting to and communicating with the DB of Serbia, the president of your republic sent a letter to the president of Serbia claiming that forces under the control of the DB of Serbia had pointed weapons at him and threatened him at a border crossing between Serbia and the RSK, and you never learned that that letter had been sent. Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't remember seeing this letter before today.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Neither seen it, nor heard about it, nor learned about it in any way. Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean this report that we have on our screens right now?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Learned of the existence of this letter from Martic to President Milosevic and the rest of the Serbian leadership.

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I really can't remember the report. He would write things often. By looking at the formulations contained in this report, I simply can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Could we, please, have 65 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Farr, could I? Did Mr. Martic tell you that he thought that Kostic was involved?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, he did say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And what explanation did he give in respect of the involvement of Mr. Kostic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He, too, was taken by surprise because he was on good terms with Mr. Kostic. He was given that information from the 11th Corps command stationed in Vukovar. As I said a moment ago, we too expressed disbelief at Mr. Kostic being the organiser behind it all because he was in Slavonia, not in Baranja. He did tell us that they were some -- Kostic's men from the DB of Serbia. But we were taken aback by that information. And he did tell us the story in exactly the terms that we see written in this report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you say, He did tell us that they were some Kostic men from the DB of Serbia, are you referring to Mr. Martic? Was Mr. Martic telling this or ...?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Martic said that. And he was referring to the information he got from the 11th Corps. The next day, Mr. Kostic himself denied it, as much, to me. He stated that he had no part in that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Therefore, the influence on the territory of the RSK by the DB of Serbia was not only rumours but was even discussed in this context. Meaning that Mr. Martic believed that there was DB of Serbia involvement in the matter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've repeatedly said that in that period of time, Martic was not on good terms with Mr. Stanisic. And in his view, that was possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So it wasn't just -- just rumours. It was even expressed by the then-highest authority in the Republic of Serbia Krajina.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But all that was not confirmed to us in certain terms, we considered to be rumours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But earlier you were asked whether you remembered any person, any specific person. And you could have answered that even Mr. Martic, at a certain moment, said this. Because your testimony was that you were -- that you have no -- you had no recollection of anyone saying this but it just being rumours. You remember that that was your testimony? But now you adjust that answer by saying that Mr. Martic, at least at one point in time, expressed as his view that Kostic and the DB of Serbia would have been involved in the attack -- or the arrest of him? I'm again seeking whether this is correctly understood. You -- I see you're nodding yes. Then I would like to remind that you're supposed to tell us the whole truth. And Mr. Farr may proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Farr.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir, this letter refers to the kidnapping of minister of the interior Ilija Prijic. Around the end of August 1994, Minister Prijic publicly stated, in fact, at a press conference that he had been kidnapped by four paramilitary soldiers in Borovo Selo, put in a car, and released several hours later in a forest near Bijeljina. He publicly accused Radoslav Kostic of being behind the kidnapping and also publicly said that Radoslav Kostic worked for Serbian state security. That's all correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that incident as well. I also remember the press conference. I don't remember all the details, but I know that he also accused Kostic. And it was, in fact, this very minister of the interior who was the cause of that conflict with Martic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Could we now please have 65 ter 6372 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir, this document is a report of the RSK RDB in Knin dated 28 July 1994. And as you can see, it's addressed to the commander of the Main Staff of the SVK. And if we could have the next page in English and zoom in on the signature in the B/C/S version. It appears that this document was signed for you by someone; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Could we please return to page 1 of the English and zoom out on the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: I'm just going to read a portion of this document. The subject line is: HV or Croatian army activities. And the document says: "On 27 July 1994 we received the following urgent dispatch from the Republic of Serbia DB department: "We have information that a Croatian army special purpose unit is located in the Nustar village sector, training for a helicopter assault. The helicopter assault is planned in the following sectors: Bridges on the rivers Danube at Bezdan and Bogojevo." And then the document goes on to give more details about the assault. I'd just like to read to you a portion of your testimony on Thursday. And this is transcript pages 16907 to 16908. The discussion was about written reports or communications from the DB of Serbia to you. You said: "We didn't receive reports about internal political matters of Serbia. The reports that the Serbian DB sent to us in Knin had to do with specific developments that they would draw our attention to. It was a wide range of issues. I don't know how far you would want me to explain it to you. I didn't need to inform the president of the republic or anything of that sort. Those were issues that related to the service." And then my next question was: "Were some of them military matters? Your answer was: "No, never?" "Q. So the Serbian DB never sent you a written communication regarding military matters that might be relevant for the SVK; is that correct? "A. No. I had never received a report that would relate to anything contacted with the SVK. "Q. Do you have any knowledge of anyone in your service ever receiving information from the Serbian DB and forwarding it to the SVK? "A. I don't remember anything of that sort." Sir, this document contradicts your testimony, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This isn't a document or a report related to military matters. This is a report from an agent in the field sending information about the movement of troops. Precisely for that reason, we forwarded that information in full to those who were charged with military issues. So the Assembly of the RSK cannot discuss these issues of assessment, how realistic this is, or whatever. That's why we would fully convey this information to the army. Not because we considered the information to be of military nature but because of who the information might be important for. Perhaps we were at cross purposes or we didn't understand each other when you were asking me about military matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir, I did my best do make sure that that didn't happen and that is why I asked you the last question, which was: Do you have any knowledge of anyone in your service ever receiving information from the Serbian DB and forwarding it to the SVK? To which you answered that you didn't remember anything of that sort. Are you now saying that that answer was not accurate?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Your question had only to do with military issues. The issues that I considered to be of military nature were never forwarded by myself or anybody else. This is part of routine reporting. For instance, when the Glina centre would send information to Knin, if I wasn't there, the deputy, if he thought it might be interesting for the Main Staff because it had to do with the defence of the RSK, the deputy had to forward it just as it is. So we wouldn't extract information or make a summary of it. We would forward it to the army as is, for them to see how relevant those issues would be. But we never dealt with military issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I tender this as a Prosecution Exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 6327 will receive P3077, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, I should have jumped up earlier and I should have jumped up earlier with the previous exhibit. Would the Prosecution indicate the purpose of the exhibit? Is it for impeachment purposes?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: It's for impeachment and for substantive evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Then I would object to the latter. I don't object to it to being used as impeachment, but I do object to it being used as -- for the truth of its contents. The Prosecution have used it for a very specific purpose. We have all seen that purpose. It is for Your Honours to evaluate whether that purpose was effective or not. But to then introduce it for the contents but without giving any indication whatsoever as to its probative value or its relevance --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, this raises a matter which is often on my mind, Mr. Jordash. If you say for the substantive value and not only for purposes of challenging the reliability or the credibility of this witness, then, of course, that raises a series of questions, the first being was this -- because we're talking about the letter sent to -- are we -- the previous one, the letter --

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the letter is in evidence, just to avoid any confusion on that point. P987 is already in evidence. The letter from Martic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. It's this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: It's this proposed exhibit that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This proposed -- we're now talking about the one now?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then I'm back in --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, that was my fault.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Our understanding is that the close co-operation between the DB and all of the armies is contested. The relationship between the DB and the military has certainly been almost the theme of this case, so it's certainly relevant to that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You would say --

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: That's why we would tender it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Farr apparently has a double reason to tender this document. First, to challenge the credibility and reliability of this witness is; and, second, to establish that there was a type of exchange of information or at least receiving information from the DB of Serbia, which he considers relevant in the context of establishing what the role of the Serbian DB in the events in the RSK were.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, if I could just add also the relationship between the Serbian DB and the RSK DB, the RSK DB acting as a conduit between those two.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And there's clear distinction here. One is that the Prosecution, we accept, could not have predicted that this witness would testify in the way that he has. Therefore, we don't object to the use of the document to impeach that testimony which they couldn't predict. But as Mr. Farr has indicated and very clear, the issue of co-operation between the DB and entities such as these dealt with in the document have been a live issue from the moment the indictment was drafted. The Prosecution ought to, having decided what their case was against the DB and against the first accused, ought to, if they wanted to rely upon this document, have put it in their initial evidence. So that we, during the Prosecution case, during the Defence case, could have adequately dealt with the issue. Now all we can do is rely upon what Mr. Draca has said and we can rely upon the future witnesses called by Mr. Simatovic's team. What we cannot do is counter this evidence through the last three years of the trial. That's the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll consider it. The document will --

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Farr, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Just except that -- a few further submissions on that point. Your Honours observed, in paragraph 14 of your decision regarding the admission of evidence in the cross-examination of Defence witnesses, that the real test is one of sufficient connection to the witness's evidence. This is a document that the witness acknowledges was signed for him. It's something that was perhaps not important enough to be included in our case when Mr. Draca was not going to be a witness in this case. Mr. Draca now has been a witness in this case. He has testified for a considerable period of time. The need to contextualise his evidence is all the greater. And also, as you observed, it is consistent with the spirit of 90(H)(i) to admit Prosecution documents in support of their case if they're sufficiently connected to the witness's evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: If Your Honours' decision was intended to remove any restriction on the Prosecution tendering exhibits, except that the Prosecution establish that the proposed exhibit has a sufficient connection to the case, then there are no evidential rules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's not what Mr. Farr says. Mr. Farr says --

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
